title: Six directions
hookLine: young Sigala bows to the six directions; the Buddha gives the bow a meaning
carry: each direction has a face in it

lines: EAST, SOUTH, WEST, NORTH, BELOW, ABOVE.
cards: Early morning, outside Rajagaha. A young householder named Sigala has bathed, and still in wet clothes, with wet hair, he raises his joined hands and bows. To the east.
The south. The west. The north.
Below. Above. Six directions, one after another.
The Buddha, walking into town for alms, stops and asks what he's doing. Sigala answers simply: my father, as he was dying, told me to honor the directions. So I do, out of respect for his words.

teach.h: HE DOESN'T TELL HIM TO STOP.
teach.b: Here's what the Buddha doesn't do. He doesn't tell Sigala to stop, or call the custom empty, or his father wrong. He says: that isn't quite how the six directions are honored in the noble discipline.
Curious, Sigala asks: then how? Please teach me. So the Buddha keeps the bow and gives it a meaning.
This is the Sigalovada, the advice to Sigala, the thirty-first Long Discourse, which an old commentary calls the householder's discipline.
First he clears the ground. A wise person avoids four ways of acting that stain a life: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct and lying.
He avoids four motives for doing wrong, which open tomorrow, and six ways wealth leaks away, the day after. Only then does he return to the bow.
The six directions are six relationships. East, the direction of the sunrise, is your parents, who came first. South is your teachers.
West is your partner and children. North is your friends. Below are those who work for you.
Above are the spiritual teachers in your life. Honor each of them, he says, and each will care for you in return. A grieving son's ritual, done for love of his father, isn't thrown away.

teach.h: THE SAME BOW, WITH FACES IN IT.
teach.b: The same bow, the same six turns.
Only now each direction has a face in it.

how: Buddhist teachers teach the Sigalovada Sutta to lay people as a guide to family and social life, and some use the six directions as a way to remember the relationships it describes.

o: six relationships, each one a direction
six sacred places a pilgrim must visit
six daily prayer times set by a teacher

s: the Buddha tells Sigala to stop bowing to the directions
he keeps the bow and gives each direction a meaning.
Sigala bowed because his dying father asked him to
he honored the directions out of respect for his father's words.
in DN 31 'below' stands for those who work for you

games.q: you're the Buddha. a young man is bowing to the six directions because his dying father asked him to. what do you say?
o: that the custom is empty and he should stop.
that this isn't quite how the noble discipline honors the directions, and when he asks, teach him.
games.why: he keeps Sigala's practice and fills it with meaning: six directions become six relationships.

practice: If you're able, face east, the morning sun's side, and with joined hands or a simple nod honor your parents, or whoever raised you.

Turn right to the south for your teachers, behind you to the west for your partner, children and household, left to the north for your friends, then down for people who work with or for you, and up for anyone who has guided you in what matters most.
A face for each, then sit.

wordCard.voice: Six directions. In DN 31 Sigala bows to them for his father's sake, and the Buddha makes them six relationships: parents, teachers, family, friends, workers, guides. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali disa: direction, quarter. Sigala bows to the six disa.

carryVoice: Your line: each direction has a face in it. The bow stays; its meaning grows. That's day five hundred sixty-six.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 31 (Sigalovada Sutta), the opening scene and the six directions
